note: Phase 1, airport. City acquired the Islands in 1867 and divided the land into lots; the first summer cottage community was on the west side; timeline: '1870-80 Summer homes established on the island. Cottages from Hanlan's Point to Centre Island'. Airport construction from 1937 infilled Hanlan's Lagoon, so the cottage community on the Western Sandbar had to go: residents could move their cottages further south at Hanlan's Point or to Algonquin (Sunfish) Island, where streets were laid out in 1938 for 31 cottages moved by barge. No source gives a year for full build-out; built_to is the end of the timeline's decade.

Conflicting count for the airport removal: 'In 1937... The lagoon that separated the Western Sandbar from the main Island was filled in to construct the Toronto Island Airport. This project also involved the removal of 37 cottages located north of Turner's Baths.' Built years repeated from the Toronto Islands article, not stated here.

Second conflicting count: 'The 54 cottages and their cottagers were moved to today's Algonquin Island (then named Sunfish Island).' The article gives no year for the move itself; gone years are the airport construction span it states (approved 1936-37, seaplane base 1938, runways and terminal 1939). Built years repeated from the Toronto Islands article, not stated here.

Phase 2, what remained after the airport. In 1956 the Islands went to the Metropolitan Parks Department under Tommy Thompson, whose park program 'included the demolition of all existing homes and legacy amenities at Hanlan's Point'. 'In the spring of 1962, the dance hall at Hanlan's Point was demolished, along with the houses' (the dance hall, a remnant of the amusement park, had been shuttered in 1949). Number of homes not stated. Built years repeated from the Toronto Islands article, not stated here.

Timeline: '1870-80 Summer homes established... Cottages from Hanlan's Point to Centre Island'; large Victorian summer homes on the Centre Island lakefront followed the Royal Canadian Yacht Club's move in 1881. Island-wide peak in the 1950s of some 630 cottages and homes; Metro Parks 'started to demolish homes and cottages' in 1955 per the article body, 1956 per its timeline; by 1970 only 250 homes, on Ward's and Algonquin, 'had escaped the bulldozer' and the 1970s saw no further demolitions. No source gives a count or end year for Centre Island alone, nor a year for full build-out.

Metro approved the park plan in February 1956 and began clearing 'more or less immediately'; leases were terminated as they came up and the land razed; the main street, Manitou Road (movie theatre, restaurants, boat rental), was demolished. 'By 1963, about 370 homes remained on the Island, most of them east of the Avenue of the Islands. Approximately 100 more were removed by the time the demolitions were halted.' No year given for the end. Built years repeated from the Toronto Islands article, not stated here.

2014 Heritage Toronto plaque 'Residents or Parks?': 'As early as 1880, homes and businesses lined the streets of Toronto Island from Hanlan's Point to Ward's Island. Before the Second World War, there were more than 600 leased residences.' Metro, established 1953, bulldozed residences and businesses as leases expired; 'By 1960, one-third of all buildings had been demolished'. The plaque gives no start year for demolition other than 'shortly after' 1953, and no build-out year.

Manitou Road, the main street. First store opened 1884 (William Clark); by 1905 it was 'the business street of Centre Island'; by August 1914 it 'boasted a wide range of services' (quoting Sally Gibson, More Than an Island). 'By 1959 the buildings on the street were demolished to make way for... the Metro Toronto Parks Department.' Opened via the Wayback copy of history.torontoisland.org (live site blocks automated requests); post is 'Brief History of Manitou Road, Centre Island' by Edward Guthrie, 2014.

2014 Heritage Toronto plaque 'Manitou Road': the main commercial street of Centre Island, originally Middle Road; a freight wharf was built in 1905 and business 'expanded in the following decade' (general store, butcher, dairy, laundries, several hotels; later a casino, bowling alley and movie theatre). 'In 1956, Metropolitan Toronto Council expropriated Centre Island for the creation of Toronto Island Park. Many of the businesses were demolished and Manitou Road was replaced by a concrete pedestrian walkway' (Avenue of the Islands). No demolition end year on the plaque.

Canadian Encyclopedia gives decades only: 'In the early 1950s, 8000 people lived on Centre Island, but its summer resort hotels, theatres and stores were demolished in the late 1950s and 1960s to make room for parkland. Since 1956, the remaining residents have struggled to save their homes.' gone_from/gone_to are that decade span, not exact years; no build years stated.

Ward's Island. William Ward opened Ward's Hotel in 1882 (closed and demolished 1966). 'In 1899, there was a colony of eight summer tenants on Ward's Island'; by 1913 the city organized the tents into streets 'and the tents eventually evolved into a seasonal cottage community' (no year given for the cottages, so built_to is blank). The community survives: 'There are 262 residential properties on Ward's Island and Algonquin Island as of late 2018', secured by a 1981 Ontario law and the 1993 Toronto Islands Residential Community Stewardship Act (99-year leases).

Algonquin Island, formerly the sandbar Sunfish Island, enlarged by land reclamation. 'In 1938, streets were laid out to accommodate 31 cottages that were moved by barge from Hanlan's Point.' No source gives the year the island was fully built up. Survives: 250 homes on Ward's and Algonquin by 1970, 262 residential properties as of late 2018.

Phase 1. In 1880 Ned Hanlan built a larger hotel 'along with rudimentary amusements'; the Toronto Ferry Company bought the site in 1892 and after the 1897 land reclamation 'opened an amusement park and the first Hanlan's Point Stadium'. The park's own Wikipedia article says only that it was built by the Hanlans 'in the 1880s' and gives no opening year. The 1909 fire date is from that article (next row).

Phase 2. 'A fire on August 10, 1909, destroyed the hotel, the wooden stadium and all but five concession stands of the amusement park'; park and stadium 'were rebuilt in time for the 1910 season'. Declined after Sunnyside opened in 1922; sold with the ferry company to the City in 1927 (the Toronto Islands article says 1926, when 'most of the rides were shut down'). 'The park was demolished in 1937 in order to make way for the Toronto Island airport.' Operated 'from the 1880s until the 1930s'.
First stadium: 'erected in 1897 at Hanlan's Point' for the Toronto Maple Leafs baseball club, who played there until 1901. 'Destroyed by a fire on September 8, 1903.'

Second stadium: 'rebuilt and reopened on May 24, 1904'. 'In 1908, the stadium was replaced with Maple Leaf Park', opened May 12, 1908, and the Leafs returned. 'Destroyed by a fire on August 10, 1909.'

Third stadium (Hanlan's Point Stadium, over 17,000 seats, architect Charles F. Wagner): first baseball game May 9, 1910. Babe Ruth's first professional home run here September 5, 1914. 'The Maple Leafs left... after the 1925 season. In March 1927, the parks commissioner... requested tenders for the demolition of the bleachers.' 'The field remained in use until the construction of the Toronto Island Airport in 1937.' The article does not say when the grandstand itself came down; the Toronto Islands article says airport construction 'led to the demolition of the stadium'.

'In 1937, construction started on a new airport on the site of the park and stadium'; land reclamation joined Hanlan's Point to the Western Sandbar by infilling Hanlan's Lagoon. 'The airport opened in 1939' as Port George VI Island Airport. The airport article adds: seaplane base first used 1938, paved runways and terminal opened 1939.
